question: A 6-week-old infant is diagnosed with primary congenital glaucoma. Corneal diameter is 13 mm bilaterally and IOP is 32 mmHg. Which is the most appropriate initial management?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Timolol is sometimes used as a temporising measure pre-operatively but is NOT first-line definitive treatment. Systemic absorption in neonates can cause bradycardia and apnoea — it must be used with extreme caution if at all.

Correct. Surgery — either goniotomy (if the cornea is clear enough for gonioscopic visualisation) or trabeculotomy (if the cornea is hazy) — is the definitive first-line treatment for PCG. Medical therapy alone cannot reverse trabeculodysgenesis.

Acetazolamide may be used as a short-term bridge to control IOP before surgery, but surgery — not medical observation — is the definitive treatment. Long-term medical management is not an endpoint in PCG.
Laser PI relieves pupil block in angle-closure disease. PCG is caused by trabeculodysgenesis, not pupil block, so LPI has no role here.

overallFeedback.feedback: In PCG, the treatment of choice is surgical angle surgery (goniotomy or trabeculotomy). Medical therapy may temporise but cannot correct the underlying trabeculodysgenesis.
Well done. Remember the cardinal rule: in primary congenital glaucoma, surgery (goniotomy or trabeculotomy) is first-line, not medical therapy.
